projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Hugh William Ostberg was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Today is November 7, 2002. This recording is taking place in the reading room of the Herbert Hoover Presidential Library in West Branch, Iowa. Today I am interviewing Hugh William Ostberg. His current address -- he was born on March 16, 1926. His current address is 1876 330th Street, Madrid, Iowa 50156. My name is Sylvia Ferguson and I'm the interviewer. I am the education assistant at the Hoover Presidential Library. Mr. Ostberg, please state for the recording what outfit you were in.

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: When I first went overseas I was in the 6th Armored Division in the 44th Infantry Battalion.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: And what was your highest held rank?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: With that division, PFC. Private first class was my highest.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: And where did you serve?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: In Luxembourg, Germany, France, Belgium.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: And what armed conflict were you in?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: I was in the last few days of the Battle of the Bulge and I was in the Battle of the Rhineland and Battle of Central Europe.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: And then you were in another war?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: I was in the Korean War. I stayed in the Reserve when I got out of the Army in 1946 and I got called back in 1950 for a year and sent to Japan. Didn't get to Korea.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: I was drafted.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: And where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: I was living in Madrid, Iowa, Boone County.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: And why did you join?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Well, I got drafted and I didn't have much choice.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Okay. Why did you pick the service -- well, I guess you answered why you picked the service branch.

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: They gave me a choice of the Army or Navy. I said Navy. They said you got the Army. They weren't putting many in the Navy at that time.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in the service?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Very much.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Do you want to tell us a little about that?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Well, about the first ten days was in the reception center just kind of getting acquainted with things and then we were sent to Camp Hood, Texas and I was put in 17 weeks of infantry combat training and that was a lot of walking in the hot sun and digging foxholes and learning how to handle the M1 rifle machine guns, hand grenades, bazookas.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Do you remember when you -- when you where exactly you went then after --

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Yes. In our 16th week we were on bivouac, and which means we were out -- camping out for a couple of weeks. They came out and got us one night and said there's been a breakthrough in Europe and they need you right away. And so it was that breakthrough turned out later to be known as the Battle of the Bulge. They were going to send us home on oh, about the 23rd of December. But it's so foggy the planes kept getting grounded, so on Christmas day of 1944 they put us on a train and sent us back home for four days, flew us to Fort Meade, Maryland, and from there we went to Boston, got on the Ile de France, a luxury liner, which had been converted to a tube ship and sent overseas. We landed at Scotland, came down to Southampton a couple of days over to Le Havre sat in the harbor there about five days and unloaded. And then got on train boxcars, about 32 of us in a boxcar and rode in those for three days. The snow got deeper and deeper. We tried to heat it with a barrel, but it gave us more smoke than it did heat. The train took us to northern part of France and then we rode the back end of a truck in the snow storm to Belgium, Luxembourg and joined the 6th Armored in Luxembourg. And I got acquainted with a boy, Ken Schaefer, on the ship and he came from Amana Colonies and he spoke very good German. He was also a teenager like me and we got put in the same squad together and we were there a few days and then eventually got into battle.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: And what was your -- your assignment I guess you would say?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Well, it started out they took us one night and we walked to the German border, which is about a mile away, and got down to the Our River which is on the border of Germany and Luxembourg. [Coughs.] Excuse me. And we -- they put us in an empty building there. I think it had been a chicken house. We stayed there the rest of the night and then early in the morning before dawn we crossed the foot bridge which meant we went into Germany and went up into a hill. We were right on the edge of the Siegfried line and we got shelled and one of the guys got hit by a machine gun and then we went -- we stayed there that night and we got relieved the next day or two and went back in to Luxembourg for a few days. So that was our first couple of days of combat.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Were there many casualties when you were in Europe?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Not that particular time, but there had been quite a few before we came to the outfit and then there were a few as we went on deeper into Germany and we had a few more. Would you like to know from there on?

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Yes. Please go on.

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: So we came back into Luxembourg and we were there a couple of days. We stayed in a house and there was a man lived there with his three sisters. He had lived in Dakota for, oh, 30 years or so and he'd come back to fix his sister's house. And he got trapped there and he never got back to the state. So he was interesting to talk to. Then we went back down the Our River a little farther south and spent a few days in a house down there. And then one morning we crossed the river again and the lieutenant told us that our assignment for that day we were to take 10 or 20 pillboxes in the Siegfried line and he said when we got across that our artillery had laid down a barrage for 20 minutes to soften them up and then we'd got in. So we got over there and they started -- our artillery started bombing them, but they started getting too close to us, so the lieutenant called for the telephone to hook onto the radio. I took it up to him and he got the artillery stopped and then we went in and started taking the pillboxes.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Can you describe what they were, how they looked?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Yes. A lot of them were built right into a hillside and they were about at least six-foot thick of concrete, the walls were, and then the dirt was piled on and grass growing over it, so airplanes couldn't see them too good when they tried to bomb them. And they had a steel door on there and they were a pretty good size. They had bunks in there and they lived there and it -- the artillery and the bombs could shake them up pretty bad, but generally not harm them, but it was very nerve-racking to them.

So after we took those, we pushed a little farther in to Germany then, and we had a lot of different experiences there. We keep taking other objectives as they came along and some of these experiences they might have been kind of serious at the time, but some of them we laughed at later on. One I always think about is when we'd go into a town, we would search every house to make sure no German solders are hiding. And one night we were taking this town and we went into this big two-story house our squad leader sent.

The assistant squad leader and myself to the basement to check out down there. And we could hear voices down there and we pushed the door open. There stood three German soldiers and sitting all around the room leaning against the walls are a whole lot of old people, evidently had gone down there for protection from the artillery and when I saw those three Germans, I was the first one in the door, the three soldiers, I pointed my rifle at them, told them, get their hands up in German. And this one said, "But we have no arms." And when they said "arms," I thought he meant he had no guns and that he was trying to trick me.

And I said, "Look, buddy, I don't care what you don't have, I told you to get your arms up." And the little old lady that lived there, she came over to me and she could speak English and she says, "But they've been injured in the war. They have no arms." Well, two of them had lost an arm and the other one had his in a sling, but had coats over them and I couldn't tell that. So they were trying to hold their belongings with their good arm and then I saw what they meant. I felt sorry for them.

They were -- they were the enemy, but they were just young guys like myself wanting to be home. So we took them prisoner and my assistant squad leader after that, quiet time sitting around, he looked over at me and started grinning at me and he'd say, "Look, buddy, I don't care what you don't have," kind of and then we could laugh about it.

It was sometimes not a laughing matter at the time. Some of the -- the experiences that might find interesting. We took a pillbox one day and we were standing up in front of us several feet and our lieutenant was hollering to one of the tankers way over on another road, pretty soon our squad leader motioned for the lieutenant to keep quiet and come over to him and he came over. He pointed down there and here we were standing on top of another pillbox and didn't know it. So we took care of things there then and pressed on farther.

Also one night after we had pushed I think it might have been that same night after we pushed the Germans back quite a ways we were dug in what we called outposting in our platoon. It was their turn that night. We dug foxholes and for protection in case they were drop artillery on us and we just got settled in there and it's dark in the wooded area and pretty soon a loud speaker, we heard a loud speaker in a German voice, he said "Achtung," which is German for attention.

And I thought hearing the German voice I was afraid that we had been surrounded and then he went on to talk, he says, "I'm a German. I was taken prisoner today," and he said, "I was treated right and I'm going to announce to my buddies over the loud speaker who might be in the area to hear me, tell them how to surrender, get rid of their helmets and their guns, come in with their hands up and I'll tell them that I was fed good today, treated right, and so if any of them come in surrender," he says, "Please, please don't shoot them. Just take them prisoner."

So I heaved a sigh of relief when I found out that we were not surrounded. There were times when you hear of sometimes of friendly fire killing your buddies. This didn't happen, but one time it could have. We were riding on our half-tracks, armored division each had infantry had rode in half-tracks when we could, and we were going into town, but our column was stopped. Pretty soon one of the machine guns started firing into the hillside. There's hillside up on both sides and -- and when that one started every machine gun in the outfit opened on both hillside.

Finally got the command to stop firing and found out there was a trigger happy tank destroyer man that had seen a deer and he was shooting at the deer. But what could have happened later on our own troops from another division came marching down both sides of the road down the ditch, and if they started firing the deer at that time, we could have shot some of our own people. Fortunately that didn't happen.

And then there was another time my buddy and I while we were all -- they started shelling us again. We went in a big field there and started digging foxholes for protection, but there was nothing around to put over the foxhole to make a roof. So I told my buddy we're not -- these aren't going to do us any good. We just run up toward that town and we ran.

There's a -- there was a wooden fence, but had little spaces about like that, but we squeezed through those and when we got through them, there was a kind of a mound made out of brick, thick walls and about maybe eight feet high and around several feet. It looked like good protection, so we ran in there.

There there were ten German soldiers and they're on their way in to surrender, so fortunately they'd gotten rid of their guns and we took them prisoner and sent them away. And then there's a house close to the -- to that area and some of other boys went over there. About that time a German jumped out of the upstairs window and they searched the upstairs and found a radio up there. And he's the one had probably been directing their artillery on us, so we got that stopped. But there's surprises quite often.

We crossed the Rhine River on a platoon bridge riding in a half-track and our -- our general was there waving us on with his cane. They told us that the night before that some of the Americans that had been there said the German SS troopers were in that town where they crossed the river and they'd all gotten drunk and was going up and down the street firing their machine guns. Well, that -- that was the night before we got there thankfully. But we pressed on a few miles more and pulled in an area, a big wide open area and we were going to spend the night there and when we did a couple of the boys from another squad went into the woods to kind of search those out.

We heard a couple of shots and pretty soon here these same two guys came back marching about 30 Germans between them and what had happened when they got in the woods, they saw a few of the Germans. They jumped behind the tree and started firing and when they did, these 30 guys stood up and all surrendered, so they came bringing them out and the next -- we stayed there all that night. After it got dark we could look back toward the town where we had just crossed the Rhine and we saw a lot of tracer bullets going up into the sky, so we knew they were shooting at an airplane. Pretty soon we saw the tracer bullets coming down, so we knew this airplane was shooting back at them.

Anyway, the next morning they had an artillery gun in a village right close there and they started firing armor piercing shells to try to knock out our tanks and half-tracks and any vehicle. And luckily when they didn't hit anything, they didn't explode. They would just hit the dirt and a little dirt fly up, so we didn't have to worry about shrapnel. So that gun finally stopped and we went on into that town and evidently they had retreated from there, so we didn't meet up with anyone there. There was a German plane flew over. It was a recognizance plane, I think, and one of our guys fired and they hit B.A.R. at him, but it was one that he had supposedly fixed and it didn't work very good. I don't think he even came close.

And then there was -- well, one day we got separated from our outfit we were riding along the German autobahn and pretty soon we started receiving fire, artillery fire and sniper fire from the left and they -- some of us hopped off of the half-tracks and ran for the road, the side of the road and others stayed on. Meanwhile, all the other vehicles took off, but at the same time just peppering that wooded area with machine gunfire. So about eight or ten of us got separated from the outfit and we ran across this field, my buddy and I there's a little depression there in the dirt and we always heard in training to look for an area like that, that might save your life.

So we did and then pretty soon the snipers started shooting at us, so Tony and I got up and ran into the woods and there we found these other guys of our outfit. And I said we can't stay here. If they send any mortar or artillery fire they'll hit the trees, it'll explode above us. And a couple of guys had an armored car that had been hit and it was down there by the road. And he said we've got smoke grenades. We'll go down and set those off and make a smoke screen for you and they did that and fortunately the smoke went the direction that we wanted to go.

So it starts spreading out that way and we started walking that same direction as the smoke rose up and we went higher up in the hill. Went a little ways and we came back down the hill, we were in the wooded area by that time and just as we hit the road, here came one of our Jeeps and one of our recognizance cars and they said hop on and really hold on, he says, we're going to have open it up. [Coughs.] Excuse me. They got guns trained on the next stretch they said. So we hopped on the back and really held on. They opened up the speed and fortunately there was no fire and we got to the next town, found our outfit and joined them up again. Did you have any questions?

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: No. Were you awarded any medals or citations during the time?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Well, they -- I might sign up for bravery. They -- they awarded you ribbons, you know, and like for theaters you serve in. You get combat ribbon and I mean good conduct and they combat infantry badge for after you've been in the combat for one month, they made you PFC, and gave you ten dollars a month more. But a while back I found out that it you if you sent this one place, you could get the medals that represent these ribbons and ribbons represented.

So I wrote to there and they sent me some and they sent me a bronze star and it had my name on it and I asked my wife and I told her I said, "I don't know why they sent me a bronze star." So I saw one of the guys I got acquainted with, who has written two books about the 6th Armored Division, and I met him in Des Moines a while back and I told him, I said, "I got my medals and ribbons," but I said, "They sent me a bronze star and I don't know why because I never earned one."

And that was generally for doing something. He says, "Yeah," he said, "They came out with a rule that if you were in the combat infantry in the Battle of the Bulge everyone got a bronze star." So it wasn't anything great I did. It was just according to their rules, I guess.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Now, in those days how did you stay in touch with the family? Do you want to mention about your family? You were just out of high school, were you in or --

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: -- did you leave school?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: No. I graduated in May and then the draft board got me in August. In those days mail was the only way to keep track, keep in touch until after the war had ended and eventually you could call home. I went -- I ended up in Paris and I got a furlough to Switzerland and I called from down there.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Tell us about what the food was like. I suppose --

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Well, it depended where you were. With the 6th Armored our particular company it wasn't the best, but I ended up like I say about the last year in Paris and they had French people cooking for us. We ate pretty good.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Did you have plenty of supplies? Did you have everything you needed?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Yes. I don't remember ever running short of ammunition or hand grenades or anything like that. That did happen at times to some outfits. And if we -- if our kitchen couldn't keep up with us, then we ate C-rations and K-rations. On the train we ate frozen C-rations.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: How did people entertain themselves? You had some time to do -- to do that?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Well, while in combat they sit around and when you had the spare time. But after I got back to Paris, they'd have stage shows and acrobats and things like that in Paris at the theater. And you could, you know, catch a train and go here and there. There's no TV in those days either.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: And you mentioned you went to Switzerland?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Uh-huh. Got a week furlough there, beautiful country. Of course, the war was over then. I was noticing here in another note here sounds kind of funny now, but they came and got us one night when we were still in combat and said we got 20,000 Germans trapped in the pocket and only one road out and we're going to go out and block off that road. You imagine how we felt trying to block off 20,000.

Well, we went up there any got set up in the road and the lieutenant gave a buddy and me a bazooka and put us by the road. I didn't see how much good that was going to do on one of their tiger tanks. Fortunately again they never came that way. The next morning they did send in some mortar shells and then that finally stopped and they also had a loud speaker out there to tell them how to surrender if they wanted to. Because I remember lying down on the bail of straw there and going to sleep and I started to wake up, I was almost scared to wake up.

I didn't really know where I was right then, but pretty soon our lieutenant came by and said consider yourself relieved. That is our platoon because they weren't coming or else that had gone another way. But you never knew what to expect. And there was one night we were in taking another town. Some of us had gone in that house, that big house there for protection. Pretty soon I heard the explosion outside. Well, it was a German 88mm artillery gun that fired at us and they exploded out in the street and the 88s you couldn't hear coming until they there were. You just hear a quick noise and a big explosion. They can fire them pointblank and shortly after that they had exploded, the door opened, and two of our guys came in.

One out of our squad had shrapnel in his shoulder and the other one was wounded real -- very badly. I mean you couldn't see. It was dark. You didn't turn or dare light any matches and he was groaning very bad. By that time I turned around on guard duty and I was gone an hour. When I came back that one man had died and they took the other man back to the hospital for his shoulder.

A buddy, a couple of my buddies, both from Iowa, they were under a blanket when that happened. They were -- they were lighting a cigarette I think. They didn't even hear the explosion. And I think it's that same town that after that happened we heard there was a big field again going to the south of us and across the field there was a road. We could hear a vehicle. We didn't know what it was, so the lieutenant took our squad.

Our lieutenant was a brave man. Sometimes I thought he was too brave, but he took us over to see what it was. Come to find out it was one of our own armored cars and they had a 37-millimeter gun and they had seen us probably the outline because it was real dark and they had that 37-millimeter gun pointed at us. They wondered who we were and we wondered who they were, so our lieutenant hollered to them and we went back and joined our outfit. But another thing that is kind of funny after you look back.

One day is our column was stopped on the road, we looked up and saw two airplanes. They looked like P-51s, our own plane, and they were starting to dive in on us out of the sun which was a trick both sides used hoping that coming in out of the sun we couldn't see them and when they did again they had machine guns and opened up the sky was just full of tracers and when they saw that the planes stopped diving and started climbing and they dipped their wings and they saw then that we were American and they dipped the wings which meant they were friends. And a few minutes later they came back on their way back to the field I suppose. When they got close to us, they started dipping their wings right away.

But when that was all happening one of the guys on our squad and everyone thought they were P-51s or looked like it. He went running over to the side of the road and he got down by the tree and he was hollering P-51, P-51, but at the same time he was crossing himself. I suppose he was saying a prayer in case he was wrong.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: What did you think of your officers or your fellow soldiers?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Most of them were pretty good. Like I said we had a brave lieutenant. He was -- he was good, he didn't send anyone out to do something that -- he was always the first one out. Most of our guys were good too. We had a couple that deserted us when it get dangerous and then come back, which we didn't appreciate, of course. But when I got put in to an office there after the war and we had a good captain, a good lieutenant, good guys to work with. Most of all they were all pretty nice.

I might tell you how I ended up in Paris. We were getting awfully close to Czechoslovakia and one night we were going to have to go across the bridge there in this town and we had gone in the building for protection for a while because every so often the Germans would shoot up a flare over this bridge and fire their machine gun across the bridge and fire an artillery shell into the town. And I heard our lieutenant telling our squad leaders said we're going to have to go across and he said so far everyone that's been hit has been on the right side of the bridge, so we're going to have to go around the left side. Law of averages.

And I was getting -- getting sick right then. I didn't know what it was, but I knew I wouldn't be able to run and that's what we were going to have to do according to the lieutenant. So, anyway, some of it's kind of dim in my memory, but they did have us -- I went back to where the half-track drivers were staying and spent the night there. The next morning I got up and my side was real sore and I thought I had pulled a muscle and I could hardly climb into the half-track when we went to catch up with our men.

So when we caught up with them, found out that Kenny Schaefer, the one that I had gotten acquainted with on the boat and we got put in the same squad, he had been hit in the arm and the foot. So where as we left -- joined the outfit together, we left together. And they took me to the battalion aide station and our new doctor there had not arrived yet, so they brought a captured German doctor to examine me in the ambulance. He said it was appendicitis. And so they took me and three captured wounded German prisoners the four of us in this ambulance and we went so far and we stopped at. I think it must have been a German hospital, a civilian hospital, and unloaded those three Germans and they took me to -- to a field hospital.

They had so many stops and they examined me. It was -- it was appendicitis, so then they put me in an ambulance asking if I could sit up and I could. Had one guy on the floor who had been in a tank destroyer that tipped over and he was still in shock. The guy next to me had been hit by machine gun in the arm. The other one, I forget. So we rode on that pretty bumpy roads because some bridges had blown out and they ran the field hospital that's set up in tents like you see on "M*A*S*H" and they took me in there and I went there was Schaefer laying on the stretcher. He was pretty well doped up because of his injuries.

And so they gave me cot and said you can sleep here tonight and then they'll take care of your appendix in the morning. But that army cot is real luxury to me. And I went to sleep, didn't wake until morning, and they had gave me breakfast. It shows the difference in the way they do things now. About noon they came and got me and gave me a spinal and took my appendix out there, so I was awake for the whole thing and in a lot of pain.

So I was there about eight days and they flew a bunch of us back to a hospital in Paris and we spent about five weeks there. Everyone that went in there, so many of them, ended up with something that they didn't go in with. A lot of it was yellow jaundice, dysentery, and things like that. So when we got out or when I got out, they took five of us and a -- and a captain and they organized a discharge center because at that time people with 85 points could get out and stay overseas and they had a job, a means of support.

So I spent the last, a little better than a year, in and around Paris. Meanwhile, the Germans quit while I was in the hospital. I remember looking in toward the city of Paris and seeing all the fireworks going on celebrating. And so I was there until June of '46 and my turn came to go home and came home in '46 and I foolishly stayed in the Reserves; although, I didn't attend meetings. But later on I was called back to -- '50 we -- '50 to go to the Korean War.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Do you want to tell us something about that?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Well, they sent me to Fort Lewis, Washington for what they called three-week refresher course, and then we were to go over to Korea and we put in the fighting. Well, I had been on sick call and they had set up appointments and they were so busy there. I think it's Madigan General Hospital that they couldn't get me in for about three or four weeks. So there I was lucky there because I get -- I got pulled off of orders to go to Korea. By that time they had a general hospital Reserve outfit from Washington, D.C. that they were trying to bring up to strength and sent to Japan to take care of the wounded that has come back from Korea. So I got put in there and sent to a town near Osaka, Japan. So I never had to get in combat in Korea.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: What were your duties during the time you were in Japan?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Well, I was in the morning report sanction, which kept records of all of the men, where they were, and where they were temporarily assigned. So I had an administrative job then which was a lot better. Of course, that's what I had in Paris right after the war and in both cases I was staff sergeant there. There was more chance of advancement. So after almost a year I was -- they'd start send us reserves back to the States replaced us with regular Army. So I was back home then in 1951.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: I supposed from both -- both wars?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Yeah. The first one was Fort Sheridan, Illinois I had come back from Europe and caught a train from Chicago, was met by my folks in Des Moines on the train. And the second coming from Korea I got out of Camp Carson, Colorado and caught the train and my mother and dad and the preacher's wife and my future wife, Donna, who was there to meet me and it was a great day.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: And then did you after -- after you got home from World War II did you go to work or back to school or what did you do?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: I went to American Institute of Business and studied accounting and worked in that area for a while and then that's when I was called back for the Korean War and then I came back and we got married.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: This is after Korea?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Or after the Korean War, I should say. And did you -- did you go to school on the GI bill?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Yes, uh-huh. That was handy. It seems like they paid us $85 a month or something like and all our expenses.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Now, you mentioned your one friend that you met. Did you have other close friends from the times you were in?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: I did. I didn't really keep up with them. This one man that was from Iowa, he -- I looked him up one day down around Burlington and then he came and visited us once and I haven't heard from him since. But he was awarded the Silver Star while I was with him. His name is Leon Hoffman and he came to me one night when we had taken some pillboxes and said the lieutenant wanted him to get five guys to come back and get some rice and so we could eat. So I was one of the five he choose and we went back and got the rice and brought it back and, but that night he made five trips from the headquarters up to the front lines and found out later that during the time he was doing that, Germans were running patrols through our lines and he made these five trips and the lieutenant put him in for a bronze star and when a higher up officer read the letter, he said that I should be worth the silver star. So they gave him the Silver Star instead and I was glad to hear that because he -- he certainly earned it.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: How did your service and your experiences affect your life? Do you think that had a strong effect?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Oh, I'm sure it probably did. Up to that time the only time I had been out of state was to Missouri one time and here I had been in all those countries and seen a different way of living. I know it taught me to respect the United States and appreciate it more.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Were you able to share your stories with your wife and family?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Most of them.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your thinking about war about the military in general?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Well, I'm not sure. I'm not sure what I -- what I thought about the military before I went in. It was a great experience. You wouldn't trade for it, but you wouldn't want to go through it again.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Have you attended any reunions at your --

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: No. In fact, I didn't know that they were organized until they were about three years from disbanding and how I found out, this boy, Kenneth Schaefer, that got shot in the arm I looked him up a few times over in Amana. He stills lives there. And, of course, he's not a boy anymore as I'm not. But I first looked him up, he told me that our division was organized, and so I wrote to him and I joined him, and Kenny and I we've gotten together a few times since then. He's meanwhile recovered from his injuries.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to add that we haven't covered?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: I probably pretty well covered it. I did have an experience there -- I don't know -- one night again. We did a lot of it at night which is good. They couldn't see us. We were to stay in this house and there was a bed there and two beds and that was -- that really looked good. Just about getting ready to settle down and they came and got us and said we had to go take the next town and they said we're go down the middle of the road because they thought the recon men had said that the ditches were booby trapped. So we went down the middle of the road and pretty soon as we got close to that town the German came walking down the middle of the road hollering for Willie and Rudy. They didn't know we were anywhere around and -- and so the lieutenant motioned for us to get off to the side. Of course, we had hoped we were passed the booby traps, if any. And so we got down in the ditch on both sides of the road and he came and walked by our lieutenant, walked by our squad leader, walked by Kenny, who they kept close to the front because he spoke such good German. He walked by me and he was probably only about eight feet from us, if that far, and he -- as he passed each of us and our lieutenant came out of the ditch and came up behind him and I say he took care of him. And then we went back up toward the town. Oh, our squad leader, our platoon leader he called in the ditch and he saw what he thought was our squad leader, took a hold of him by the foot and he said, "Jim, Willie and Rudy got up and surrendered." So anyway we took them prisoner and then we went in toward the town and they set up machine gun and the road forked off like that and they sprayed and we sprayed the machine gun fire down there. The lieutenant I think showed a hand grenade. Well, the boys behind us didn't know what all was going on. They heard the machine gun and the hand grenade and they thought it was one of their tanks firing at us. There was pandemonium then. They were running all across the field in the dark. So we got stopped and everyone stopped and we backed off a ways and called for our artillery and the lieutenant said send in five rounds of white phosphorus, which is very intense fire. You don't want to get burned by it. So we laid down waiting pretty soon our artillery sent white five rounds of white phosphorus on the way. We heard him fire one. We heard it go over our hand and heard the second one and the third and then the fourth. They were all going into town. Here come the fifth one and we could tell it was going to land short. After hearing a few you know about and it short. We heard it hit the ground, but it didn't explode, and we went on back to the town that we were supposed to stay in and we got to sleep in those beds after all. The next morning another outfit went to us and took the town and as we went through that town, there was a house on fire. The roof was burning. The rest of it I don't think was burning, but they were made to -- the walls were made about that thick made of rock and stone. And so we went through the town. There's a big heavyset German lady on one side of the street, and one on the other, and they ran together and threw their arms around each and they were crying. I suppose the house belonged to one of them. But, you know, at times like that you feel sorry for the enemy. Felt sorry for them, felt sorry for those boys that had lost an arm and most of them didn't want to be in fighting just like we didn't. War is a terrible thing.

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: Can you think of anything else you want to mention?

sp.speaker: Hugh William Ostberg
sp.p: Oh. I mentioned the Ile de France that we went over on they took the Queen Mary and Queen Elizabeth too and made two transports. I think there's about 12,000 on there and they said if you fall overboard we won't stop and get you. We'll throw you a lifesaver and you'll last about 30 minutes in that cold water and a lot of us were sea sick for about two, three days which is a very miserable thing. I got sea sick going back home on the boat. I get sea sick going to Japan for three days and then I enjoyed the trip. Coming from Japan I was fortunate to be one of them that got to fly. I don't get sea sick -- or air sick. So a few weeks after we had been married I picked up the Des Moines paper one day and there was a picture of the Ile de France that I'd gone over on. And some movie company bought it for a picture and in the movie they sink the ship. And it made me think about when Kenny and I were on that ship. It was so crowded that they had bunks, just railings with netting over it, about five high, and you just slid into the bed like a -- an envelope and you could hear -- it was right against the side of the boat. You could hear the water sloshing around there and we were way in the bottom deck and I often thought that if a torpedo comes in, it would come right in bed with us probably. That's how I met Kenny. He was a great guy. And I've met the guy that has written -- I don't know if you heard the book entitled, "I Was a Teenage Infantry Replacement." It was one of the guys from our outfit. I didn't know him at the time, but when I bought his book and read it, found out that he and I were on the same ship at the same time, but 12,000 people how do you meet? But combat infantry is about as bad as you can get. You live like an animal sometimes. You dig a hole and two guys to a hole, only one can sleep at a time in case of them pulling a counterattack. If you could find anything after you got the hole dug, then if you find logs or any kind of tin or something to lay over the hole and then pile the dirt on that. Sometimes you could get maybe a direct hit by a mortar shell and it wouldn't, you know, it wouldn't kill you. Sometimes you weren't that fortunate. I -- at one time I told you about the first day of combat on the Siegfried line. My buddy pointed over and said, "Do you see a German standing outside that pillbox?" And I -- I don't know if my eyes weren't good then or what. I didn't wear glasses. I couldn't even see the pillbox and we were all out of water, so I took several canteens down to the foot of that hill to fill them up and when I got down there and I started filling them up. After I got them pretty well full, they started shooting at me with a, what they called a German burp gun. It was a machine gun that was so fast it almost sounded like the burp. They said when the first one hit you, they'd all hit you. If the first one missed you, they'd probably all miss you. It made a cracking sound as it went over your head. So I decided I had enough water. Evidently it was that guy that my buddy had seen that was doing the firing. Always -- our ladies of the church there they had a missionary society that met once a week and they had an agreement between them that every day when the noon whistle had blow, most small towns have a dinner whistle that they would all say a prayer for the boys in the service. And I often thought about that and I thought maybe their prayers were just causing that bullet to just veer off. I always give them the credit and say serve a great God. Do you have any questions?

sp.speaker: Sylvia M. Ferguson
sp.p: I think... [inaudible]. So we want to thank you very much.
